cards.source_text: Scientists have described a species of tiger cat that was previously unknown to science. From Bolivia’s Yungas cloud forests, it is the first discovery of a living novel cat species in more than 100 years. The tilcayo (Leopardus tilcayo) takes its species name from the name locals already had for it. Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer who discovered the species and co-author of the Current Biology paper that describes it, said the name honors traditional knowledge in the region. The tilcayo is smaller than a domestic cat at 1.4 kilograms (3 pounds). It has rounded ears, a slender body and a coat with large spots. “I have the honor of naming a cat, and that’s a really big thing,” Nogales-Ascarrunz, who is also a researcher at the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz, Bolivia, told Mongabay by phone. For decades, researchers lumped small spotted cats across South America under a single species name: Leopardus tigrinus or tiger cat. However, evidence had been mounting for years that the group might contain several species. In the article published on Sept. 17, researchers unwound the species’ genetic web and confirmed at least four distinct species. Many newly recognized small cat species result from this kind of taxonomic reshuffling: Researchers find a subspecies is actually a distinct species; or two different species that had been lumped together are separated. But the tilcayo was different. Researchers knew a cat occurred in the Yungas cloud forests, but it had never been formally described. Research had a breakthrough when a Bolivian family brought their pet tilcayo, named Tigrino, to the Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary near La Paz around 2017. The family had rescued Tigrino as a kitten, thinking it was a domestic cat, but began to suspect it was something more wild when the tiny feline started stalking their neighbor’s chickens. Testing on Tigrino, and on one hair sample from a rescued tilcayo that had been rehabilitated and returned to the wild, showed that L. tilcayo was farther removed from other tiger cats than anyone had expected. Genetic analysis showed that the species had never been sampled before and matched no known species. “We expected the tilcayo to maybe be a subspecies, or something like that, because it was different,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “Then we saw it was 1.4 million years ago that this cat separated from the others, and that was amazing because we didn’t expect that much separation.” For reference, human

cards.source_text: Sebastian Thrun, a computer scientist, entrepreneur, and adjunct professor at Stanford University (whose projects have included Waymo, Google X, Google Street View, and more) has launched a study to evaluate “the capabilities and limitations of AI systems for writing English-language philosophy.” Called PhilosophyBench, the study is focused on “whether AI can generate novel philosophical ideas and develop them clearly with depth and sophistication, not merely summarize existing views or apply existing philosophical theories.” The advisory board for the study includes philosophers Ned Block, Nancy Cartwright Ruth Chang, Kit Fine, Gideon Rosen, Jonathan Schaffer, Crispin Wright, and Linda Zagzebski, as well as computer scientists. The project involves developing “an independent academic benchmark against which claims about capabilities in AI philosophical reasoning and writing can be evaluated. If a new AI model comes out and claims are made about its philosophical capabilities, we hope that this study will provide an independent methodology that can judge those claims.” The questions to be addressed by the project include (according to its FAQ): - Can an AI generate novel philosophical ideas and develop them clearly with depth and sophistication? - Can an AI generate essays that could be accepted to a philosophy journal, or earn admission to a leading philosophy PhD program? - To what extent does providing human philosophy BAs and PhDs access to AI tools change the quality of the philosophical writing that they produce (this is called an “uplift” study)? - Given that many frontier AI models are already pre-trained on an extensive set of philosophical work across human history, what limitations, if any, prevent frontier AI models from producing philosophical work at the quality level of the best philosophical work in human history? - When AIs write philosophy, are there any patterns in how they write that reveal anything about AI alignment, particularly when AIs are asked to produce novel arguments? - What, if anything, might the philosophical capabilities of current AI systems tell us about how future AI systems might develop? The project is currently looking for people with philosophical training to help with the project (“professional philosophers, graduate students, or advanced philosophy undergraduates, as demonstrated through formal education or other appropriate evidence”). Further details are at the PhilosophyBench site.

cards.source_text: Listen to this essay 22 minute listen Jürgen Habermas died on 14 March 2026, in the German town of Starnberg, aged 96. Every fall, from the mid-1990s into the late-2000s, he would come to Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois to teach and give talks, a visit that a dedicated group of students looked forward to every fall term. The year that has stayed with me is 2004, when he taught what he’d spelled out in Between Facts and Norms (1992), his opus applying his theory to democratic politics. Law, philosophy, history, political science: students spanned many disciplines to come watch the famous German scholar every week, dressed in Wrangler jeans and a tweed jacket, expose his theory of deliberative politics in his unmistakable nasal voice, thick German accent, and impeccable English. Max Weber and the Frankfurt School, which were intimate to him, since he’d been Theodor Adorno’s research assistant in the 1950s, came to life in his speech and then in schemas and figures in chalk as he theorised about them. I understood almost none of it at first: words I’d read were coming to life in the room, spoken by their author, and still not resolving into sense. After several lectures, the shape came into focus: this wasn’t just Between Facts and Norms being rebuilt in public, but decades of work arriving at a single place. Since The Theory of Communicative Action (1981), Habermas had been arguing that reason survives in modern life only as something people do together, that is, by giving each other reasons and staying open to being moved by them, rather than by force, money or tradition. Between Facts and Norms was that idea turned toward law and democracy directly: a state counts as legitimate only when its laws could in principle be justified to everyone bound by them, through exactly that kind of open exchange. I’d watched that argument take root in a decades-long intellectual history. Thinking is a practice, it involves owing each other explanations, questions, answers. It is not a fast process, and doing it in public, out loud, in front of a room, is what makes it worthwhile. I attended all of Habermas’s seminars during my time at Northwestern with great interest and, to be honest, a sense of awe. cards.source_text: In this short video, Bill Hammack, an engineer and professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, details the extraordinary making and tragic ending of the British airship known as R101. Conceived in 1924 and first flown in 1929, R101 was intended to fly a regular route from England to India. Hammack uses archival images and his own deep research to trace the engineering and history of this remarkable vessel, which the British government planned as the flagship of a fleet that would criss-cross its then-sprawling empire. Those ambitious plans were abandoned after the airship crashed in France in October 1930, killing 48 of the 54 people on board. Hammack offers a riveting peek into a brief moment in aviation history – one ended for good by the crash of the Hindenburg in 1937 – when it appeared as if commercial airships might become a regular sight in skies across the world. The video accompanies Hammack’s book Fatal Flight: The True Story of Britain’s Last Great Airship (2017), which is available as a free audiobook at his website. cards.source_text: Critical theorists like Theodor Adorno may have overreached in claiming that all mass culture is mediocre, mechanized propaganda made to justify the status quo. But that doesn’t mean they were entirely wrong. Over and over we see even the most subversive art, literature, film, and music has a way of being tamed and Bowdlerized. Global mega-corporate industries don’t need to censor what they don’t like; they only need to buy it, rebrand it, or price it out of reach. So what? Why do we need challenging, independent art when we have endless entertainment? Is the concept a nostalgic, elitist, Eurocentric idea? Artists have justified the need for art since antiquity, with poetic and logical arguments of every kind. But Dada artists of the early 20th century broke ranks, building their movement on the insight that no defense could possibly mean anything when it came to art’s purpose, especially in the face of the technocratic slaughter of World War I. When the hyperrationalism of modernity led to mass death and destruction, the only humane response was to declare war on rationalization—to “destroy the hoaxes of reason,” as French artist Jean Arp put it. “For the disillusioned artists of the Dada movement,” the Museum of Modern Art explains, “the war merely confirmed the degradation of social structures that led to such violence: corrupt and nationalist politics, repressive social values, and unquestioning conformity of culture and thought.” Dada took a combative stance against, for one thing, the insistence that art justify its existence to win establishment approval. “All activity is vain,” declared poet Tristan Tzara in his 1918 “Dada Manifesto,” including the “monetary system, pharmaceutical product, or a bare leg advertising the ardent sterile spring…. The beginnings of Dada were not the beginnings of art, but of disgust” with the ossified culture of the “nice, nice bourgeois,” who would preserve at any cost “the possibility of wallowing in cushions and good things to eat.” “And so Dada,” wrote Tzara, “was born of a need for independence, of a distrust toward unity.” Such declarations aside, the movement was decidedly unified in its aims. “For us, art is not an end in itself,” poet Hugo Ball wrote. “It is an opportunity for the true perception and criticism of the times we live in.” This critique required new experimental techniques that deformed and repurposed the technologies of mass culture. cards.source_text: Image by Library of Congress/Carl Van Vechten, via Wikimedia Commons Many a foreigner has visited England and found it an unexpectedly surreal place. Some of that effect has to do with encountering familiar icons — Big Ben, double-decker Routemaster buses, Marmite — in cold, damp reality. More of it may be induced by the country’s simultaneously thoroughgoing cultures of normality and eccentricity, an endless source of inspiration for Monty Python’s Flying Circus and much other British comedy since. Yet England came relatively late to Surrealism, or rather, Surrealism came late to England. When the International Surrealist Exhibition opened at the New Burlington Galleries behind London’s Royal Academy in the summer of 1936, the Manchester Evening News decried it as “a travesty of everything that’s decent.” Naturally, the show was a smash hit. On display was work by artists including Pablo Picasso, René Magritte, Max Ernst, Alexander Calder, Giorgio de Chirico, Marcel Duchamp, Alberto Giacometti, Paul Klee, Man Ray, and Salvador Dalí, who turned up in person to deliver a lecture on “Authentic Paranoiac Phantoms.” In order to “descend to the subconscious” with a properly Surrealist literalism, he rented a diving suit and helmet from a local outfitter for his appearance. (You can see an actual image from 1936 here.) “The diving suit had extremely heavy lead shoes which I could barely lift,” he writes in his autobiography, as translated by Haakon Chevalier. “I therefore had to walk very slowly, leaning on friends who helped to move me, as though I were completely paralyzed, and thus I appeared before the audience holding two luxurious white Russian wolfhounds on a leash.” Only after he’d been talking for a few minutes did Dalí realize that “it would be impossible for me to deliver my speech through the glass window of my helmet. I am perched atop several tons of iron, with 80 horsepower at my command. This part of farming is straightforward – even a mechanically challenged tree-hugger like me can manage to depress the clutch, shift into second, and ease the throttle forward. The tractor’s tall, deeply treaded tires churn, revolving into a smooth spin. Everything is spinning: fans, belts, alternator, the driveshaft, axles. I don’t understand the mechanism fully, yet the tractor and chopper and I are propelled forward across the knee-high whiskers of a coarsely bearded cornfield. It is Indian summer in southern Wisconsin. My wife and I and our young son live here on her family’s farm. Both of us are employed off the farm, but on weekends and many evenings I am an apprentice to my father-in-law, David. Today, we are taking advantage of a brief period of warm, dry weather. Winter is approaching, and I could be spending the day beside our woodsplitter – the gasoline-sipping, hydraulically heroic mechanism that makes it possible to put up several cords of firewood quickly each year – but that work can wait until the cool, sunny days of fall are shoved aside by the relentless spin of the earth into darkness, sleet, snow and frozen ground. The wall of tall green corn that stood here this summer has been transformed by fall and harvest. Little is standing after the field was stripped by a seed-combing combine. The mechanical tornado flails so loudly behind me: wailing against the air, grinding off the root-buttressed corn-stalk stumps, sucking up spent leaves and stripped cobs. In my wake, dry corn litter passes through the chopper like water compelled into frothy turbulence, falling again into an even, silent surface that hides so much activity below. No time to waste – the weather is expected to hold for another day, and I need to cover the field before the light fails this afternoon. Tomorrow, David will rake this chewed-up detritus into windrows and then come back for another round to bale them up. While it is good to leave some of this thatch on the field – to keep a roof over the soil and guard against erosion by wind and rain – we can afford to borrow some of this, which also makes good straw. cards.source_text: There is a photograph of Tomi Adeyemi staring out from the cover of her new novel, The Siren. It is an arresting image: her face fills the frame, unsoftened by a smile, her piercing gaze fixed directly on the viewer. “It’s terrifying – like the Mona Lisa, staring at you everywhere,” she says, laughing. Using an author portrait on the cover of a novel is highly unusual, and a decision that Adeyemi says is a statement of ownership. After 12 years spent inside the world of Children of Blood and Bone – the first book in the YA trilogy that made her a literary star and its film adaptation which has become a source of profound distress – Adeyemi wanted this book to belong unmistakably to her. “It was an intense choice, and I think it’s because I needed people to see me in this one,” she says. “I’ve had so much success, but it was also done in a way where so many people’s interpretations were put on to who I was.” The recent public fallout from the forthcoming film adaptation may have drawn attention, but the 33-year-old Nigerian American author had already spent much of her adult life being watched. Children of Blood and Bone, her 2018 debut, became a publishing phenomenon, netting a major seven-figure deal and debuting at No 1 on the New York Times young adult bestseller list. Its story of Zélie, a young woman fighting to restore magic to the kingdom of Orïsha, was inspired by West African mythology and offered something Adeyemi had craved as a child: a dark-skinned Black girl at the centre of an epic fantasy. The success brought its own mythology. Adeyemi was not merely a successful young writer; she became, she feels, a symbol of what the next generation of Black YA literature might be, something she felt the weight of acutely. “I felt pressure to be the perfect dark-skinned Black girl, to be ‘Oprah good’,” she says. “This was the biggest YA book deal in history, not just for a female or Black author. And so few of us are given a shot at all, so for the last 12 years there’s been this sense of carrying everyone.” Readers would tell her what the book had meant to their children. “You have no idea what this did for me,” they would say. Such responses were moving, but also difficult to know what to do with. Now, with The Siren, Adeyemi has moved from epic fantasy to something more contemporary. cards.source_text: The recorded DJ mix—as both musical format and unit of cultural currency—has come full circle over the past four decades. In the Wild West era, sets captured off the soundboard at raves and nightclubs circulated as bootlegged cassettes. Then came the mix CD boom of the 1990s and 2000s—an explosion of series like X-Mix, DJ-Kicks, Global Underground, and fabric, whose fractal paths through electronic music’s tangled genre tree mirrored the scene’s rapid worldwide spread. The 2010s brought DJ mixes online as sites like SoundCloud gave even the most parochial sounds a global footprint. By the 2020s, Boiler Room and YouTube were pumping a firehose of audio and video from the world’s DJ booths to fans’ screens, definitively dissolving club culture’s status as a velvet-roped sanctuary accessible only to those in the know. The wheels of steel turned out to be perfectly adapted for the grist of the content mill—last year, the dance-music website Resident Advisor celebrated 1,000 installments of its weekly mix series—but, as in so many other arenas, the internet has proved the ultimate leveler, facilitating and accelerating an endless array of series and club recordings that has devalued the form. These days, even the most avid dance-music fan isn’t so much spoiled for choice as flattened beneath an avalanche of options. The Wild West turned into a teeming megalopolis, but when it comes to attention spans, most mixes play to tumbleweeds. No score yet, be the first to add. Sasha and John Digweed’s Northern Exposure, released in 1996, is a relic of an era when mix CDs mattered—when a well-executed set could serve as a snapshot of a genre’s evolution, freeze it in time, maybe even lay the ground for a whole new movement. Lean, atmospheric, and relentlessly percussive, the UK duo’s double-disc set helped canonize the sound of progressive house, a subgenre whose name Mixmag’s Dom Phillips had coined four years earlier, calling the “thoughtful, uplifting and trancey” style a homegrown response to American house and techno. “It’s simple, it’s funky, it’s driving, and it could only be British,” he wrote—yet no one could quite agree on its true definition. Northern Exposure both complicated that assessment, fueled by a healthy variety of underground American and European sounds, and streamlined the sound itself, tightening the parameters of an ill-defined, often contested style. cards.source_text: Joy Division stood at the intersection of austerity and ecstasy. Restraint to the point of severity is a core component of the band’s sound, look, and legend: four dour, unsmiling young men from Manchester in nondescript clothing, creating spare paeans to alienation and oppression, all under the watchful eye and glacial hand of producer Martin Hannett. Their album covers are colorless, and the accompanying music feels black and white and gray all over. Yet at the same time, Ian Curtis was one of the most nakedly emotive singers of his time. Throughout Joy Division’s concise discography, his warped crooner’s voice feels alternately choked with rage, despair, and, on rare occasions, even joy. Many of his songs end with him chanting the same lyric over and over—“So lose some sleep and say you tried!” “God in His wisdom took you by the hand, God in His wisdom helped you understand!” “Dance, dance, dance to the radio!”—as if desperate to make himself heard. No score yet, be the first to add. The 19 live recordings collected on Eternal (Live) begin in March 1979 and end just days before Curtis’ suicide in May 1980. Calling a 14-month span in a short-lived band’s run eternal would seem like overkill in most cases. But if the continued, pervasive influence of Joy Division on musicians of all kinds isn’t literally everlasting, that’s only because we haven’t gotten that far yet. The music that Curtis, Peter Hook, Stephen Morris, and Bernard Sumner created casts a dark and enduring shadow. Even for longtime fans, Eternal offers new insight as to why Joy Division’s legacy has lasted: This band is fun as hell. That, too, runs counter to expectations; any time I mentioned to a friend or family member that I’d been assigned to listen to 19 Joy Division concerts in a row, they expressed concern for my well-being. But mainlining hour after hour of the foursome’s thrilling live performances turns out to be anything but dreary or depressing, whatever the subject matter of the songs themselves. If you ever attend a Gilla Band show, you will know instantly which their fans prefer. Discomfort is the baseline goal for a band that weaponizes its instruments to such earsplitting magnitudes that they rarely resemble the tried tools of rock music: guitar, bass, drums. “The trick,” bassist Daniel Fox said in a recent interview with Pitchfork, “is to be louder than everyone else.” This is a wild but typical understatement from the humble Irish quartet, which also comprises vocalist Dara Kiely, guitarist Alan Duggan Borges, and drummer Adam Faulkner. Volume—blown out to extremes or dampened before a deafening blast—in no way explains Gilla Band’s precision as songwriters, producers, or engineers. What may sound like chaos is the product of meticulous layering and sonic manipulation that smudges the lines between post-punk, noise, no wave, industrial, and techno. On their exhilarating fourth album, Pugnello, Gilla Band sharpen their implements and go in for the kill. Sure, Pugnello is loud, but it’s the nasty textures, the colliding rhythms, the gnarled vocals, the dense details that affirm Gilla Band’s mastery of dissonance. It’s their most methodical and charged album to date. Not long after they formed in 2011, Gilla Band began experimenting with a bracing concoction of noise-punk and dance music. In 2013, they released “Why They Hide Their Bodies Under My Garage,” a cover of the post-dubstep single by English DJ Blawan. The original simmers for six minutes at a steady pace and decibel level; Gilla Band stretch it, torque it, and spike it with pedal-warped guitar that sounds more like a feat of extreme knob-wringing. Watching them perform it live is a study in tension and release, dynamics they wield like classical conductors or spring break DJs. Gilla Band withhold the drop for a torturous length of time, whipping the crowd into a frenzy of potential energy. Just before they kick up the volume and crash-land on the beat, they pull back to near silence, a single fret slide bridging the gap. It accounts for maybe one whole second, but that tiny bit of space is what sends limbs into motion. No score yet, be the first to add. People will call you conceited simply for having high standards, partners might act intimidated or jealous of your success, and what about the guys you’ll have to beat off with a stick when they get too attached? Such are the problems Jae Stephens confronts on her stellar major label debut, AUDACITY. Born in Dallas and raised in Los Angeles, Stephens is a Beyoncé Tumblr stan turned self-taught pop artist. She found early success as a songwriter, helping to pen tracks for the likes of Normani, Ashanti, and Jennifer Lopez, but she’s been releasing music under her own name since 2017. On 2024’s SELLOUT EP, she hit her stride with flirty, neotraditional tracks that nodded to the rhinestone shine of 2000s-era radio R&B and established her persona as an ultra-confident, playfully misandrist diva. AUDACITY speaks boldly about relationships in the voice of a woman who isn’t embarrassed to say that she’s the prize. No score yet, be the first to add. Stephens is a pop student in a way that a former stan would be, and AUDACITY reads from an encyclopedia of acclaimed Black pop artists and producers: the percussive snap of opener “Crush” recalls Janet Jackson’s new-jack-swingy “Nasty.” “Gymnastics” and “Expensive & Difficult” feel closer to Timbaland’s shuddering pop production of the 2000s and the distorted dancefloor blur of Danja’s work on Blackout. Ashanti’s “Foolish” and Willow’s “Whip My Hair” both get name-checked on “B4U.” “I Miss the City” features a blinging harp melody akin to Brandy’s “All in Me,” produced by Darkchild. She may have grown her bawdy style and pop star image through fandom, but Stephens brings her own brazen personality and winking, trollish humor. Songwriting, she recently told Rolling Stone, is “the one place I’m allowed to be the villain. cards.source_text: Tom Morello’s guitarwork across Rage Against the Machine’s four immortal albums landed a perfect bullseye in the rarefied nexus of radical creativity and rock’n’roll classicism. The elastic wah-wahs in “Bulls on Parade,” the valiant chords in “Know Your Enemy,” the laser beam solo in “Sleep Now in the Fire”—these are generational soundtracks for battering steering wheels and pumping fists. None of the subpar projects Morello did after his Wall Street-crashing rap-rock band initially disbanded—Audioslave, Prophets of Rage, the virtuous yet unmemorable protest folk he released as the Nightwatchman—came close to eclipsing Rage Against the Machine’s incendiary music and incisive political messaging, which was the culmination of four distinct artistic personalities joining forces, not just one or two visionaries directing their hired hands. Nothing Morello does now can diminish his essential contributions to RATM, and in recent years, he’s taken full advantage of that leeway. In 2018, the guitar god released his debut album under his own name, The Atlas Underground, an atrocious scramble of collaborations with dubstep producers (Knife Party, Bassnectar), radio-rock dweebs (Marcus Mumford, Portugal. The Man), and the rapper K. No score yet, be the first to add. It doesn’t feel good to rag on Morello. Inherent hypocrisies of being a self-proclaimed activist who lives in an L.A. mansion aside, his politics have been admirably consistent for all of his public life; he’s a fiercely vocal champion of socialist, anti-racist, anti-war, and pro-Palestinian causes. He’s a likeable presence in a celebrity caste rife with ghoulish sellouts, which is why it’s so disappointing that his new album, Everyone Gets Everything They Want, fails to provide anything that anyone who loves Morello’s classic work would actually want. The animals will be sterilised and permanently moved to a newly constructed sanctuary. The plan has been fiercely criticised by animal rights activists, who say the monkeys should remain roaming freely, and that less destructive options have not been properly considered. Cape Town’s baboon problem has been brewing since the 2000s, after the city stopped culling troops in the late 1990s after pressure from the public. But in the past two years it has reached boiling point. A 2025 census found that the population had grown by a third since 2000, from 360 baboons to 493, now living in 12 managed troops. As a result of the population boom, troops of chacma baboons on the city’s peninsula regularly rip off roof sheeting, sneak into unlocked cars and raid food pantries. Some monkeys are now staying up late into the night to break into homes in Simon’s Town and nab snacks from convenience stores. cards.source_text: Louise Kennedy’s life has hardly wanted for dramatic events, but the recent past has been spectacularly busy, even by her standards. You wouldn’t know it to look at her, as we chat in the sitting room of the house in Sligo that she shares with her husband, son and daughter, but this is the home that she once thought would be repossessed. The couple bought it “for stupid money” in 2007, when they also opened a restaurant, initially so successful that the only way seemed to be up. The following year, financial mayhem descended on Ireland, their customers ebbed away, and the Celtic Tiger years morphed into a country racked with job losses, bankruptcies, apparently endless debt. “I didn’t think I’d ever be able to keep the house,” she says, glancing around an elegant room dotted with beautiful objects and plants, but nonetheless relaxed and comfortable. “I’d say we only got out of negative equity about a month ago. There are probably arguments for moving now, but I’m so proud that we managed to hold on to it, I’m not going anywhere. I’m going to be carried out of here in a box.” Kennedy had been a chef for 30 years, working all over the place from Dublin to London and, for two years, Beirut, before ending up in Sligo, on Ireland’s west coast, not far from the border with her native Northern Ireland. Crucially, she had never given a thought to writing, not since a teacher had admired a poem she wrote when she was seven. Now, she is about to publish her second novel, Stations, which follows a collection of short stories, The End of the World Is a Cul-de-Sac, and her debut, Trespasses, which was shortlisted for the 2023 Women’s prize for fiction and won other prizes in Ireland and the UK in 2022 and 2023. Last year, Trespasses gained further acclaim when it was adapted for Channel 4 in a production starring Gillian Anderson as the mother of Cushla, the young Catholic teacher who falls in love with Michael, an older, married Protestant lawyer, in 1970s Belfast. It is an arresting image: her face fills the frame, unsoftened by a smile, her piercing gaze fixed directly on the viewer. “It’s terrifying – like the Mona Lisa, staring at you everywhere,” she says, laughing. Using an author portrait on the cover of a novel is highly unusual, and a decision that Adeyemi says is a statement of ownership. After 12 years spent inside the world of Children of Blood and Bone – the first book in the YA trilogy that made her a literary star and its film adaptation which has become a source of profound distress – Adeyemi wanted this book to belong unmistakably to her. items.title: Does avoiding misery make you happy?
items.summary: It might seem like self-preservation, but the results aren’t necessarily what you’d expect In Dr Seuss’s Green Eggs and Ham , the relentlessly upbeat Sam-I-Am spends the entire book badgering a grouchy, nameless narrator into tasting the eponymous dish. He cycles through one inventive but futile pitch after another – in a house, with a mouse, in a box, with a fox, on a train, in the rain – until the narrator, caving just to get some peace, tastes the dish and discovers he loves it. When my son was growing up, “Green Eggs and Ham” was my shorthand for telling him he was avoiding something he’d love if he only tried it. Of course, not every experience we fear or dread turns out to be a delicious surprise. Misery is an inescapable part of the human condition. We can’t avoid it, yet people try their hardest anyway. We cling to hope even when a situation is hopeless. We push painful thoughts out of mind rather than confront them. We struggle to control things that cannot be changed. And we go to sometimes self-destructive lengths to protect our pride from even the tiniest pinprick. These strategies may sometimes spare us pain in the moment. But while they are intended to promote (or at least preserve) our happiness, over time they have the perverse result of making us much more miserable. Continue reading...

items.title: ‘We left Ireland because there wasn’t work – and we wanted to get the hell away’: Trespasses author Louise Kennedy
items.summary: Her Troubles-set debut became a hit TV series starring Gillian Anderson. Now the novelist has returned to her teen years for a follow-up. She talks about her journey from chef to author, and how her cancer diagnosis inspired her to write Louise Kennedy’s life has hardly wanted for dramatic events, but the recent past has been spectacularly busy, even by her standards. You wouldn’t know it to look at her, as we chat in the sitting room of the house in Sligo that she shares with her husband, son and daughter, but this is the home that she once thought would be repossessed. The couple bought it “for stupid money” in 2007, when they also opened a restaurant, initially so successful that the only way seemed to be up. The following year, financial mayhem descended on Ireland, their customers ebbed away, and the Celtic Tiger years morphed into a country racked with job losses, bankruptcies, apparently endless debt. “I didn’t think I’d ever be able to keep the house,” she says, glancing around an elegant room dotted with beautiful objects and plants, but nonetheless relaxed and comfortable. “I’d say we only got out of negative equity about a month ago. There are probably arguments for moving now, but I’m so proud that we managed to hold on to it, I’m not going anywhere. I’m going to be carried out of here in a box.” Kennedy had been a chef for 30 years, working all over the place from Dublin to London and, for two years, Beirut, before ending up in Sligo, on Ireland’s west coast, not far from the border with her native Northern Ireland. Crucially, she had never given a thought to writing, not since a teacher had admired a poem she wrote when she was seven. Now, she is about to publish her second novel, Stations, which follows a collection of short stories, The End of the World Is a Cul-de-Sac, and her debut, Trespasses, which was shortlisted for the 2023 Women’s prize for fiction and won other prizes in Ireland and the UK in 2022 and 2023. items.title: ‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeys
items.summary: Two troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answer Cape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up two baboon troops coming into repeated conflict with residents . The animals will be sterilised and permanently moved to a newly constructed sanctuary. The plan has been fiercely criticised by animal rights activists, who say the monkeys should remain roaming freely, and that less destructive options have not been properly considered. Cape Town’s baboon problem has been brewing since the 2000s, after the city stopped culling troops in the late 1990s after pressure from the public. But in the past two years it has reached boiling point. A 2025 census found that the population had grown by a third since 2000, from 360 baboons to 493, now living in 12 managed troops. items.title: Country diary: I’m virtually living in the woods now. Wildlife is everywhere | Kate Bradbury
items.summary: Lewes, East Sussex: Owls, bats, badgers and countless birds are my new neighbours, but I’ve been particularly taken by a mystery tree – and its resident treecreeper I have made the woods my home, moving from Brighton to the outskirts of Lewes, where the garden backs on to the remains of an old oak wood. Here there’s a riot of wildlife: a badger that makes snuffle holes in the lawn, a family of tawny owls in the trees and a cauldron of bats in the chimney. I have plans to let the wood expand into the garden, but in the meantime there’s a mystery tree whose branches almost reach my bedroom window. It’s nearly dead, stressed from too many droughts, perhaps, or coming to a natural end. Some have suggested it’s a willow, but I suspect it’s a cultivated species I’m not familiar with.
